tag: Episode 28 Side Story · The Price of a Safe Tomorrow
title: The Price of a Safe Tomorrow

beats.t: The good luck continued for a week. Yeoni began to feel a little afraid.
The scholarship paperwork passed on the first try. The sneakers they wanted were half price. Whenever they needed it, the elevator waited on the first floor.
(Bad luck not showing up for work makes me more anxious. What kind of person am I?)
“Good fortune makes you suspicious first.”
The other world taught me that. Nothing was free except the bread.
“Still thinking about the bread bag coming back folded?”
(Yes. Did she eat it? Just return the bag? Folded so neatly, it looked like a receipt.)
I think she's afraid to receive things. Because then she has to repay them.
“People like that have usually had a lot taken from them. Or taken a lot from others.”
Could be both.
The doorbell rang. The woman next door stood outside holding a box.
Your package came to my apartment by mistake. It's yours.
Oh, thank you. Would you like to come in? Have some tea?
I'm fine. I'll leave in a moment.
Yet she did not go. Standing in the doorway, she looked inside. At the taped umbrella in the corner.
You repaired the umbrella. Instead of throwing it away.
Yes. It flipped, but it looked like it could survive. A waste to throw it out.
Seated beside the sofa, Neo looked at her. His hand tightened on the armrest.
The day that umbrella flipped was the worst day of my life. Missed the bus, got soaked, gave an app one star.
A rating?
Yes. To the universe. And the universe actually replied. Hard to believe, I know.
The corner of her mouth moved very slightly. Too brief to call a smile. Gone at once.
I believe you. The universe replies. Always late, though.
Oh, that sounds like experience.
Just saying things. Never mind.
You've been lucky lately, haven't you?
How did you know?
Written on your face. But good luck doesn't last. You know that, right?
She took a business card from her coat pocket. Gold letters on black. Tomorrow Guarantee Consultation.
A short folded contract was attached. We hold and protect your tomorrows on your behalf. No misfortune will reach you.
Leave them in our care before bad luck returns. Then you won't lose anything.
(I've seen this on the island that sold time. Blue Rabbit's contract. Read the fine print first.)
Yeoni read to the end. At the bottom, in tiny letters: During custody, the user's important decisions must be discussed with the custodian beforehand.
What counts as important? It doesn't define the scope.
Everything. Every risky decision.
So in exchange for protection, I hand over my choices.
Better than choosing and getting hurt. You're someone who gets hurt making choices. A great deal.
There was strange certainty in her words. Like someone who had seen Yeoni hurt many times.
I'll choose whether to get hurt, too. Thank you, but no.
Why? Getting hurt is painful. You don't like pain. Nobody does.
I don't. But if I only take safe paths someone else chooses, that isn't my tomorrow.
The woman opened her mouth, then closed it. As though about to argue and losing the words.
Her fingers clutched the card's corner. The paper crumpled.
Leave a debt alone, and it grows.
The room fell quiet. Goosebumps rose along Yeoni's back. That tone. That sentence. Heard before the vault on the island that sold time.
...What did you just say?
Nothing. Just something adults say.
The woman reached to retrieve the card. Her sleeve slid up.
A scar circled her right wrist, as though something had squeezed it for a long time. A thin gold cord was embedded at its center.
(A ring mark. On the right. ...The right forepaw.)
Yeoni tried to catch the memory. Black fur, golden ring, the feel of pushing with their forehead. But it blurred like wet paper.
Then Neo rose beside the sofa. He started to grab the woman's outstretched wrist, then stopped. His fingertips brushed the gold beneath her sleeve.
Neo! Don't! She's a guest!
...It's all right. I'm not hurt.
She avoided Neo's eyes, pulled down her sleeve, and stepped back.
Excuse me. I'll leave the card. Knock if you change your mind.
The door closed. Yeoni picked up the fallen card. A contract on the front. And the back.
Handwriting covered the back. Thin and neat. Every stroke pressed carefully, like writing in a ledger.
[ Don't go to the bus stop on rainy days ]
(The bus stop? Why the bus stop?)
“Can't tell if that's a warning or a threat.” Neo braced against the chair's armrest, his knuckles tense.
Could be neither. Could be concern.
“Who shows concern by offering a contract first?”
(But why the bus stop? The one in our neighborhood is just an ordinary stop.)
Yeoni looked outside. The bus stop before the apartment stood quietly beneath a streetlight. Water dripping from its roof's edge looked strangely familiar.
For an instant, someone seemed to stand beneath it, an umbrella tilted halfway. One blink, and nobody was there.
Neo. Was someone at the stop just now?
“Nobody. But I smelled rain.”
People over there did that, too. Could only express worry through a price tag.
Yeoni set the card beside their notes and added one more line. Woman next door. Umbrella on clear days. Ring mark on right wrist. Leave a debt alone, and it grows.
Before sleeping, Yeoni pressed a palm to the wall. Cold. Very faintly, paper turned beyond it. One page, then another.
(A ledger. That tiger was always writing things, too. Who owed how much.)
The sound continued a long time, then stopped abruptly. Someone caught a breath, very quietly.
The weather app sent a notification. Tomorrow: showers from three in the afternoon.
